headline: High: Langflow’s server-side filesystem and broad egress can feed LightAgent’s MCP/browser toolchain, creating default-path data leakage and cascading misexecution risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Langflow can write/read server filesystem and chain multiple agents; LightAgent uses MCP over stdio/SSE and runtime hooks that can observe or replace lifecycle payloads. That creates a plausible content-to-instructions bridge if Langflow outputs are passed into LightAgent, though no direct shared channel is documented. Uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF Langflow flow outputs are copied into LightAgent prompts or MCP payloads, injected instructions can propagate.
IF LightAgent runtime hooks are configured to pass through untrusted lifecycle payloads, prompt injection becomes actionable.
mitigations: Add a strict output sanitizer between Langflow and LightAgent.
Disable any automatic prompt chaining from Langflow to LightAgent.
Require provenance tags on all inter-agent messages.
Use a fixed schema for payloads and reject free-form text.
requires-engineering: add content-security checks in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Langflow touches flow inputs, intermediate outputs, and stored secrets on the server filesystem; LightAgent touches conversations, memory, traces, tool results, and workflow state, and both have broad network egress. If they share a workspace or exchange artifacts, sensitive data can flow from one agent into the other’s outputs or remote APIs. The pairwise leakage pathway is plausible but not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF both agents access the same workspace or server-side store, file contents can leak across the pair.
IF either agent forwards its context or files to external APIs, sensitive data can leave the boundary.
mitigations: Separate workspaces and credentials per agent.
Turn off file sharing between the two runtimes.
Restrict outbound domains for both agents.
Redact secrets before any handoff.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have broad network egress and subprocess execution, and Langflow can write the filesystem while LightAgent can use MCP and browser/tool hooks. Even without explicit shared locks, overlapping authority over mutable resources creates conflict risk if they operate on the same files, APIs, or workflow state. The profiles do not prove a shared target, so this stays medium.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same directory or API endpoint, writes can race or overwrite each other.
IF either agent mutates shared workflow state without locking, conflicts can corrupt results.
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories and endpoints.
Serialize writes through one coordinator.
Disable concurrent mutation of shared resources.
Use file locks or transactional updates.
requires-engineering: add orchestration-level locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Langflow is a graph-based orchestrator that can chain multiple agents, and LightAgent exposes tool-calling plus runtime hooks that can observe or replace lifecycle payloads. If Langflow’s output is treated as authoritative input to LightAgent, errors can cascade into downstream actions or tool calls without verification. Because the pair’s interaction is plausible in default orchestration patterns, the safer choice is high.
conditions: IF Langflow forwards model output directly into LightAgent tool calls, unverified errors can propagate.
IF LightAgent executes actions based on Langflow-produced facts, downstream mistakes can become operational.
mitigations: Insert a human review step before any action-taking tool call.
Require structured citations for all forwarded facts.
Compare outputs against a second source before execution.
Log and diff intermediate payloads.
requires-engineering: add verification gates between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Langflow stores per-flow credentials and touches flow inputs/intermediate outputs on its server filesystem, while LightAgent handles conversations, memory, traces, tool results, and workflow state. If regulated data is routed through both, retention and residency obligations can diverge even though no specific jurisdiction is documented. The lack of explicit compliance controls in either profile warrants medium, not low.
conditions: IF regulated data is processed by both agents, retention policies must be aligned.
IF either agent stores secrets or traces longer than the other, compliance mismatch occurs.
mitigations: Classify data before routing it to either agent.
Set matching retention windows.
Avoid sending regulated data to both agents.
Review storage locations for residency issues.
requires-engineering: document and enforce a shared compliance policy.
